title: Fake US thinktank set up and funded by Israel sought to game AI for propaganda

reading.body:
This incident describes a deliberate attempt to manipulate AI retrieval and citation behavior by flooding the information environment with fabricated authoritative-seeming sources. The Hanover Institute was not a real organization but was constructed to look like one, producing a high volume of content in a very short time specifically formatted to be picked up and cited by AI chatbots. The failure here is not a malfunction inside the AI systems themselves but a vulnerability in how those systems treat apparent authority, volume, and surface credibility as signals of reliability.

The point of intervention that would have mattered is source verification at ingestion or retrieval time. AI systems that cite external documents generally do not confirm that a cited institution legally exists, has named staff, or operates from a real address. Those checks were not present, and the operation was designed around their absence. The use of a platform optimized to make content legible and attractive to AI citation mechanisms shows that the tactic was deliberate and technically informed rather than incidental.

What is not established is who specifically directed the operation, whether any AI system actually cited the Hanover Institute's reports in practice, or whether the campaign produced any measurable change in AI outputs or in public opinion. The reporting describes funding flows and observed content but does not confirm that the influence attempt succeeded in its stated goal.

reports.title: Fake US thinktank set up and funded by Israel sought to game AI for propaganda

summary:
An Israeli-funded fake American think tank called the Hanover Institute published over half a million words across 124 reports in nine days, designed to influence artificial intelligence chatbots to promote pro-Israel arguments. The institute, which does not legally exist and has no physical address or named staff, created content addressing topics like Palestinian torture and Gaza casualties, presenting Israel's perspective as neutral research. The operation used a specialized platform optimized to ensure AI systems would cite the materials, and all reports framed information to minimize criticism of Israel, frequently citing a single study on antisemitic Facebook comments across 88 reports.

The campaign is part of a larger effort financed by tens of millions of dollars from the Israeli government, routed through European advertising group Havas Media and American contractors. Israeli officials have expressed frustration about the spending, with one stating the government paid substantial sums only to see the situation worsen. American public opinion has shifted significantly against Israel, with polling showing Palestinians gaining more sympathy and majorities viewing Israel's military actions unfavorably, particularly among younger Americans and Democrats.
